summary: Mission Architect is a browser game for 1–4 players that turns the abstract trade-offs of space mission design into hands-on decisions. Players choose one of three missions, each built around a real science question: spotting wildfires and crop stress from Earth orbit, mapping water ice at the lunar poles, or tracking the Martian climate. They then design a complete spacecraft – orbit, launch vehicle, ground stations, instruments, solar arrays, battery, pointing system, propulsion, antenna and flight computer – while a live dashboard shows how every choice changes budget, launch mass, power, eclipse energy, delta-v and data flow. After a flight readiness review and a Go/No-Go vote, the mission is simulated day by day, with anomalies such as solar storms, reaction-wheel failures or a solar conjunction that the responsible crew role must handle. A debrief scores the mission and explains in plain language why it succeeded or failed, so teams can improve their design and re-fly under identical conditions. Built on real orbital physics and NASA planetary data, it runs in any browser with no installation.
details:
What it does

Mission Architect is an interactive space mission design game for one player or a crew of up to four. It lets players experience a complete mission from the science question to the last downlinked bit – and understand why it succeeds or fails.

How it works

1. Choose a mission. Three scenarios with different engineering challenges: Blue Marble Watch (Earth observation in low Earth orbit – coverage, air drag, data volume), Lunar Ice Hunter (water ice at the lunar poles – delta-v, long eclipses, station keeping in lumpy lunar gravity) and Red Planet Climate (Mars climate orbiter – a 210-day cruise and getting data home across up to 400 million km). Three difficulty levels and a sandbox mode.

2. Design the spacecraft. Players choose orbit, launch vehicle, ground-station time, up to four science instruments, solar arrays, battery, attitude control, propulsion and propellant load, antenna and flight computer. A live dashboard updates with every click: budget, launch mass vs. rocket capacity, orbit-average power, battery energy needed in eclipse, delta-v available vs. required, data generated vs. downlinked, storage and a science forecast.

3. Flight readiness review. Blockers and warnings explain what is wrong and how to fix it. Every crew member then votes GO or NO-GO; a launch needs a unanimous GO, or the Mission Lead can override at a cost to the teamwork score.

4. Fly the mission. Launch, cruise, orbit-insertion burn and day-by-day operations, visualised in real time. Anomalies – solar particle storms, reaction-wheel failures, micrometeoroid hits, ground-station outages, debris conjunctions, lunar eclipses, Martian dust storms, solar conjunction and budget cuts – require a decision from the responsible role. The design decides how much each anomaly hurts: a spare wheel or a radiation-hardened computer turns a crisis into a footnote.

5. Debrief. A score out of 1,000 across five criteria (mission performance, science value, resource efficiency, decision quality, teamwork), a plain-language cause-and-effect explanation, a chart of science returned over time, a design comparison table and a local leaderboard. Teams can re-fly under identical random conditions to compare designs fairly, or share a design as a link.

Team play

Four roles with deliberately conflicting goals: Mission Lead (finish 10% under budget), Payload Scientist (return 120% of the science target), Systems Engineer (keep power and mass margins) and Comms & Data Lead (get every bit home). The best crews negotiate designs where everyone wins – just like real systems engineering.

Real physics, honestly labelled

The simulation uses Kepler's third law for orbital periods, eclipse geometry, the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, a link budget (data rate grows with antenna diameter² × transmitter power ÷ distance²), battery depth of discharge, solar-array degradation and solar irradiance at Earth and Mars. Planetary radii, gravitational parameters, solar irradiance and distances come from the NASA Planetary Fact Sheets. Component masses, costs and science values are simplified game values, and the in-game "Data & sources" panel clearly separates real data from game-model values.

Benefits and intended impact

Students, teachers and space enthusiasts can experience system-level trade-offs that are usually taught one subsystem at a time. Because every result is explained, players learn from failure – exactly how engineers learn. The game is free, runs in any modern browser, works offline and needs no installation or account, so it can be used in classrooms anywhere.

Tools and languages

HTML5, CSS3 and plain JavaScript with Canvas graphics in a single file – no frameworks, no build step, no external dependencies. Hosted on GitHub Pages; source code: https://github.com/marlonwollny-dotcom/NasaSpaceAppsChallange_Counterbirne. The demo slides were built with PptxGenJS.

What makes it creative

Instead of a quiz about facts, players are mission designers: every decision has visible consequences in a connected system. The Go/No-Go poll and conflicting role goals turn engineering trade-offs into a team negotiation, and the debrief turns failure into insight.

Factors we considered

Scientific accuracy vs. simplicity for beginners; transparency about what is real and what is simplified; fair comparison through seeded random events; accessibility (clear text labels alongside colours, keyboard-usable controls); and no NASA logos or insignia.

AI disclosure

The game's source code was developed with the help of an AI assistant (Claude, Anthropic) and reviewed and tested by our team. This is stated in the game's footer, in its HTML metadata and in the README. No AI-generated images, audio or video are used; all graphics are drawn live by code.
